# Temple Scroll Column 16 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

This log records all lines in Temple Scroll Column 16 where the three translators diverged, along with SOPHIA's resolution.

---

## 16:1 — "assembly" vs. "solemn assembly" vs. "closing assembly" — atseret

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "an assembly shall be for you" | Literal atseret tihyeh lakhem |
| LOGOS | "you shall have a solemn assembly" | "Solemn assembly" is the traditional rendering of atseret |
| PNEUMA | "hold a closing assembly" | Atseret derives from atsar (to restrain/close); captures function |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted "solemn assembly" (LOGOS). This is the established English rendering for atseret across major translations (KJV, NRSV, ESV). PNEUMA's "closing" is etymologically interesting but not standard. EMET's passive construction is awkward in English.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS.

---

## 16:11 — "Command" vs. "Give instructions to" — tsavveh

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "Command the sons of Israel, saying to them" | Literal tsav et bene Yisra'el |
| LOGOS | "Command the children of Israel and say to them" | Standard formal rendering |
| PNEUMA | "Give these instructions to the Israelites" | Natural modern phrasing |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. "Command" preserves the imperative force of tsav — God is issuing commands, not merely giving instructions (PNEUMA). "Children of Israel" consistent with Col. 15 ruling.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS.

---

## 16:13 — "set over me a king" vs. "appoint a king" — placement verb

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "I will set over me a king" | Literal asimah alai melekh |
| LOGOS | "I will set a king over me" | Standard English word order |
| PNEUMA | "Let me appoint a king over me" | "Appoint" more natural for royal installation |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The verb sim (set/place) is best rendered "set" in the context of royal installation — it matches the language of Deuteronomy 17:15. "Appoint" (PNEUMA) is acceptable but slightly more interpretive. EMET's word order is awkward.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS.

---

## 16:14 — "surely set" vs. "indeed set" vs. "must appoint" — infinitive absolute construction

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "you shall surely set over you a king" | Infinitive absolute som tasim rendered with "surely" |
| LOGOS | "you shall indeed set over you the king whom I shall choose" | "Indeed" for emphasis; preserves divine choice |
| PNEUMA | "then you must appoint the king I choose" | Modal "must" conveys obligation |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. "Shall indeed set" captures the emphatic infinitive absolute while maintaining formal register. The critical theological point — "whom I shall choose" — is preserved by all three but rendered most naturally by LOGOS.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS.

---

## 16:17 — "multiply horses" vs. "acquire many horses" vs. "build up a large stable"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "he shall not multiply for himself horses" | Literal lo yarbeh lo susim |
| LOGOS | "he must not acquire many horses for himself" | "Acquire many" is standard Deuteronomy rendering |
| PNEUMA | "he must not build up a large stable of horses" | Interpretive paraphrase conveying the military-economic concern |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. "Acquire many horses" is the standard rendering in major translations (NRSV, ESV, NIV). PNEUMA's "build up a large stable" adds interpretation beyond the text. EMET's "multiply" is archaic in this context.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS.

---

## 16:18 — "return by this way" vs. "go back that way" — directional phrase

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "You shall not return again by this way" | Literal lo tosifun lashuv ba-derekh ha-zeh od |
| LOGOS | "You shall never again return by that way" | "Never again" captures the emphatic prohibition |
| PNEUMA | "You must never go back that way again" | Most natural modern phrasing |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. "Never again return by that way" preserves the gravity of the prohibition while being clear. "Return" is more precise than PNEUMA's "go back" for the theological concept of reversal to Egypt.

**Status:** Resolved in favor of LOGOS.

---
